lesson.title: Google Cloud organizations folders projects and billing
lesson.why: Projects collect resources and quotas, but they do not isolate every inherited permission or determine every billing relationship. A clear hierarchy reduces accidental broad access and unowned spending.
lesson.what: Design a fictional Google Cloud organization with folders, projects, billing attachment, and explicit ownership. Keep financial authorization separate from resource administration.

concepts.name: Hierarchy conveys inherited controls
concepts.body: An organization contains optional folders and projects; projects contain service resources. Applicable IAM grants and organization policies flow through this structure. A role granted at a folder can affect every descendant project, so local project reviews must include ancestor assignments.

concepts.name: Projects are practical boundaries
concepts.body: Projects organize API enablement, resource identity, many quotas, and operational ownership. Separate environments when lifecycle or access needs differ. Deleting a project is a broad lifecycle action, not an appropriate shortcut for cleaning up one experimental resource in a shared environment.

concepts.name: Billing attachment is separate
concepts.body: A project can be linked to a Cloud Billing account, and billing permissions differ from project-resource permissions. One billing account can fund multiple projects. Moving billing association changes financial responsibility but is not equivalent to moving the project in the resource hierarchy.

concepts.name: Budgets inform accountability
concepts.body: Budgets and alerts help detect actual or forecast spending, but they are not automatic hard caps on resource usage. Reporting delay, shared charges, credits, and commitment allocation affect interpretation. Labels and ownership metadata need a documented strategy for costs that cannot be labeled directly.

e2e: Define teams, environments, data constraints, and owners for fictional workloads.
Place projects beneath folders matching shared access and organization-policy needs.
Connect approved billing responsibility without conflating it with administrative roles.
Apply allocation metadata and budget notifications with clear response ownership.
Review inherited permissions, unused projects, and exceptions before changing hierarchy or billing links.

tasks.name: Sketch the hierarchy
steps: Draw one organization, Production and Sandbox folders, and two projects under each.
Draw the billing account beside the hierarchy with links to projects, not as a folder parent.

tasks.name: Allocate a shared charge
steps: Assume a shared service costs 900 fictional units and projects consume 200, 300, and 400 requests out of 900 total.
Proportional allocations are 200, 300, and 400 units. These are invented accounting inputs, not service prices or proof request count is always a fair driver.

tasks.name: Trace inherited access
steps: An engineer lacks a local project binding but inherits a broad folder-level role.
Explain why checking only the project's direct bindings is incomplete. Propose reviewing the ancestor scope rather than adding another grant.

tasks.name: Write a budget response
steps: A budget crosses 80%. Assign an owner to inspect growth, confirm billing delay, and evaluate safe mitigation.
Do not automatically delete a shared project. These mock decisions do not validate actual IAM, billing, or policy behavior.

key_terms: Organization: top-level resource hierarchy entity.
Folder: optional grouping and policy scope.
Project: service-resource and operational boundary.
Billing account: financial account funding linked projects.
Budget: spending-monitoring threshold, not inherently a hard cap.
lesson.safety: Do not create projects or change billing links. Enabled services can incur charges; disabling billing or deleting a project can interrupt workloads and lose access to data.
cleanup: Retain the fictional ownership map.
No project, policy, or billing configuration was changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a project has no direct broad role grant but a user still administers it. What would you inspect?
interview_points: Inspect folder and organization inheritance.
Separate billing roles from resource roles.
Review organization-policy effects independently.
Correct the narrowest responsible scope and preserve required access.

gcp/google-cloud-organizations-folders-p.core: Google Cloud hierarchy and billing are related but distinct. Projects inherit controls from folders and organizations; billing accounts fund projects separately. Budgets notify accountable owners rather than automatically guaranteeing a spending cap.

storyboard.title: A project inherits unexpected folder access
storyboard.objective: Connect ancestor scope to effective project permissions.

scenes.title: Separate relationships
scenes.caption: Hierarchy and finance attach through different mechanisms.
scenes.narration: The project inherits applicable folder controls while a billing account separately provides its financial association for enabled services.

scenes.title: Local review misses access
scenes.caption: No direct binding does not mean no inherited permission.
scenes.narration: A project-only access review overlooks a broad folder grant, leaving an engineer with more authority than the workload owner expected.

scenes.title: Correct ancestor scope
scenes.caption: Fix authorization without confusing billing ownership.
scenes.narration: Owners review the inherited binding and narrow it deliberately while preserving the project's approved billing relationship and required operations.

lesson.title: Google Compute Engine and managed instance groups
lesson.why: A managed instance group can recreate unhealthy VMs, but a broken template can reproduce the same failure repeatedly. Useful availability depends on health, placement, and startup evidence.
lesson.what: Design a Compute Engine fleet from an instance template, regional placement, autoscaling, and autohealing policies using a synthetic request workload.

concepts.name: Templates define reproducible instances
concepts.body: An instance template captures configuration used by a managed instance group. Versioned images and startup dependencies make changes traceable. An unmanaged instance group can support grouping and load balancing but does not provide the same automatic lifecycle reconciliation as a MIG.

concepts.name: Regional placement reduces zonal risk
concepts.body: A regional MIG distributes instances across zones according to its configured policy. Distribution is not sufficient if surviving zones lack throughput or dependencies remain zonal. Stateful MIG features require deliberate configuration; ordinary recreation should not be assumed to preserve every local file.

concepts.name: Autohealing and autoscaling differ
concepts.body: Autohealing replaces unhealthy instances using configured health checks, while autoscaling adjusts desired capacity from supported signals. Load-balancer health should often detect serving failure quickly; replacement checks may need more conservative timing to avoid destructive loops during transient dependency problems.

concepts.name: Updates consume overlap capacity
concepts.body: Rolling updates use configured surge and unavailable limits. New instances must initialize, pass readiness, and access dependencies before old instances leave. Quota, image access, and address availability can stall rollout even when the template's syntax and target size look correct.

e2e: Define measured per-instance capacity, image version, state, and initialization time.
Choose zonal or regional placement from availability requirements and dependencies.
Configure distinct routing-health, autohealing, and scaling objectives.
Calculate update overlap and failure headroom within quota and networking limits.
Canary a template revision and stop on repeated startup or application failures.

tasks.name: Separate fleet controls
steps: Classify a dead VM, a healthy but overloaded fleet, and a new application release.
Assign autohealing, autoscaling, and rolling update respectively; explain why increasing count cannot fix a universally broken image.

tasks.name: Calculate a failure floor
steps: Assume nine VMs, three per zone, each serving 40 requests/second. One-zone loss leaves six VMs and 240 requests/second.
For demand 220, modeled headroom is 20. These assumed capacities are not measured Google Cloud performance guarantees.

tasks.name: Detect a replacement loop
steps: New VMs repeatedly fail a startup dependency and are autohealed into identical failures.
Check image and bootstrap changes, conservative initial delay, and dependency reachability. Pause the rollout and preserve the known-good template.

tasks.name: Plan an immutable update
steps: Draft a canary template version, synthetic request checks, bounded surge, and rollback to the previous version.
These paper steps do not validate live autohealing, quota, disk state, or IAM access.

key_terms: MIG: managed instance group maintaining configured VMs.
Instance template: reusable VM configuration.
Autohealing: replacement of unhealthy instances.
Autoscaling: capacity adjustment from demand signals.
Surge: temporary extra instances during an update.
lesson.safety: Do not create VMs or groups. Instances, disks, external addresses, load balancers, logs, and transfer can incur costs; avoid deleting shared disks during experiments.
cleanup: Keep the fictional capacity and template plan.
Future cleanup must inspect retained disks, images, and load-balancer components separately.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, autohealing recreates every VM but the service never recovers. What might be wrong?
interview_points: Inspect shared template and startup dependencies.
Distinguish application health from machine existence.
Use measured initial delays and stop replacement loops.
Restore a known-good revision and validate useful traffic.

gcp/google-compute-engine-and-managed-in.core: MIGs reconcile configured VMs, but autohealing, autoscaling, and updates are separate controls. Regional placement needs surviving throughput. A broken template can turn replacement into a loop.

storyboard.title: A bad MIG template causes repeated replacement
storyboard.objective: Show why recreation is not inherently recovery.

scenes.title: Known-good fleet
scenes.caption: Instances initialize from a tested configuration.
scenes.narration: The group creates VMs from the approved template, and application health checks confirm that they can serve requests.

scenes.title: Broken startup repeats
scenes.caption: Recreating the same configuration reproduces failure.
scenes.narration: A template revision introduces a startup defect, so autohealing repeatedly launches replacements with the same underlying problem.

scenes.title: Restore the template
scenes.caption: Recovery changes the cause, not only the instance count.
scenes.narration: Operators pause expansion, select the known-good template, and validate canary readiness before allowing the group to replace remaining failures.

lesson.title: Google Cloud VPC firewall rules load balancing and DNS
lesson.why: Google Cloud networks have global scope while subnets are regional. Routing, firewall targeting, load-balancer health, and DNS must be traced separately to explain reachability.
lesson.what: Model a two-region application using a custom VPC, regional subnets, firewall targets, and an appropriate load-balancer family without sending packets or changing rules.

concepts.name: VPC and subnet scopes differ
concepts.body: A VPC network is global, while its subnets are regional. Custom-mode networks give deliberate address planning. Shared VPC separates host-project networking from service-project resources, but this shared connectivity does not automatically grant application-level access to every resource.

concepts.name: Routes and firewalls answer different questions
concepts.body: Routes choose destination paths; firewall rules permit or deny applicable traffic. Google Cloud VPC firewalls are stateful, with target selection and priority influencing evaluation. Lower numeric priorities are higher priority in applicable rule evaluation; hierarchical and network firewall policies require their own full-context review.

concepts.name: Load-balancer families differ
concepts.body: Application and network load balancers have different protocol, proxy, scope, and source-address behavior. Backend health checks need supported reachability and correct serving ports. A frontend address existing does not prove the backend is healthy or the application path matches client expectations.

concepts.name: DNS is its own dependency
concepts.body: Cloud DNS public and private zones serve different visibility scopes. Private-zone authorization and hybrid forwarding determine which clients receive internal answers. A successful lookup does not establish reachability, and a private address does not by itself prove the application rejects unauthorized callers.

e2e: Locate client and backend networks, regional subnets, and actual resolved addresses.
Trace effective routing to the intended frontend or private destination.
Evaluate applicable firewall policy and target selection for requests and health checks.
Verify listener, backend port, health criteria, and application authorization.
Use evidence from each layer to choose the narrowest corrective change.

tasks.name: Draw resource scope
steps: Draw one VPC spanning two regions with one subnet in each and zonal VMs inside those regional subnet scopes.
Label the distinction: VPC global, subnet regional, VM zonal.

tasks.name: Work a firewall priority example
tasks.goal: Evaluate a bounded offline rule set.
steps: Assume two applicable ingress rules in the same VPC rule set: deny TCP 22 at priority 900 and allow TCP 22 at priority 1000.
Expected decision is deny because 900 has higher priority. This simplified case excludes hierarchical policies and does not prove a live firewall result.

tasks.name: Find a health-check gap
steps: A load-balancer frontend resolves correctly, but all backend health checks fail.
Inspect target ports, application binding, and documented health-check access requirements before opening every source range.

tasks.name: Trace private-name visibility
steps: A service-project VM sees an internal DNS answer while an office client does not. Review private-zone visibility and forwarding paths.
Record expected answers without probing real hosts; offline topology does not establish routing or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Regional subnet: IP allocation scoped to one region.
Shared VPC: centrally hosted network used by service projects.
Firewall priority: ordering value for applicable rules.
Backend service: load-balancer definition of serving targets.
Private zone: DNS zone visible to authorized network contexts.
lesson.safety: Do not modify firewalls or DNS. Load balancers, NAT, resolver options, addresses, and transfer can incur costs; never expose administrative ports broadly for a lesson.
cleanup: Keep the synthetic layer-by-layer trace.
No network configuration or public records were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, DNS resolves a Google Cloud frontend but requests fail. Which layers remain unproven?
interview_points: Routing and applicable firewall policies.
Listener and backend health-check configuration.
Application port binding and authorization.
Private-zone scope if clients receive different destinations.

gcp/google-cloud-vpc-firewall-rules-load.core: Google Cloud VPCs are global and subnets regional. DNS, routing, stateful firewall policy, load-balancer health, and application authorization are separate layers; inspect each rather than widening all access.

storyboard.title: A reachable frontend has unhealthy backends
storyboard.objective: Separate DNS success from backend serving readiness.

scenes.title: Resolve and connect
scenes.caption: Frontend reachability is only the first layer.
scenes.narration: The client resolves the expected address and reaches the load-balancer frontend, establishing no guarantee about backend health.

scenes.title: Backend checks fail
scenes.caption: A port or firewall mismatch blocks useful serving.
scenes.narration: The configured backend health path cannot reach the application, so a valid frontend address still does not yield successful requests.

scenes.title: Repair the narrow path
scenes.caption: Documented probe access and application binding align.
scenes.narration: Operators correct the specific backend port or health-check permission and verify application requests without opening unrelated administrative access.

lesson.title: Google Cloud IAM service accounts and workload identity
lesson.why: Service-account keys create durable credentials that can outlive workloads. Federation reduces key handling, but only narrowly bound trust and resource authorization prevent unintended access.
lesson.what: Trace a fictional CI workload through identity federation to a Google Cloud resource, distinguishing trust configuration, service-account impersonation, and target permissions.

concepts.name: IAM grants operate at scopes
concepts.body: IAM role bindings connect principals to permissions on resources and can inherit from project, folder, or organization scopes. Predefined and custom roles differ from broad basic roles. Effective access may also be constrained by applicable deny policies and organization controls.

concepts.name: Service accounts are identities and resources
concepts.body: A service account can act as a workload principal, and permissions on that account can allow others to use or impersonate it. Permission to administer a service account is different from the permissions granted to that service account on storage or other services.

concepts.name: Federation exchanges external identity
concepts.body: Workload Identity Federation trusts a configured external issuer and maps claims into a workload identity pool. Attribute conditions restrict which external workloads qualify. Supported designs can grant direct resource access or use service-account impersonation; federation itself is not a blanket resource grant.

concepts.name: Trust must be specific
concepts.body: Bind issuer, audience, subject, and meaningful workload attributes such as a repository or deployment environment. A valid token from a shared issuer does not prove it came from an approved workflow. Short-lived credentials reduce exposure time but do not compensate for an overbroad role.

e2e: Identify the external workload, trusted issuer, and stable claims available for restrictions.
Choose direct federation or a justified impersonation path for the target service.
Scope resource roles and impersonation permissions separately.
Obtain short-lived access through the supported exchange without exporting a service-account key.
Verify permitted and forbidden workload claims and target operations in a later approved test.

tasks.name: Map two authorizations
tasks.goal: Separate acting as an account from using a resource.
steps: Draw an external job impersonating a service account, then that account reading a storage object.
Label impersonation authorization on the first edge and object access on the second.

tasks.name: Work a trust decision table
steps: Assume accepted claims require issuer I, repository team/release, and environment production.
A token matching all three is a candidate; team/demo with the same issuer is rejected by the proposed condition. This is a mock decision, not proof of actual provider syntax or IAM evaluation.

tasks.name: Reduce a broad grant
steps: A CI job only reads one artifact bucket but has project Owner. Replace the design with an appropriate read-only resource scope and separate deployment permissions if needed.
Do not infer that short token lifetime makes Owner harmless.

tasks.name: Plan keyless migration
steps: Inventory callers, validate the federated path, transition one synthetic workload, and define emergency recovery before retiring an old key.
Do not retrieve or disable any actual key in this exercise.

key_terms: Service account: nonhuman Google Cloud identity.
Impersonation: authorized use of another principal's identity.
Workload identity pool: collection of federated external principals.
Attribute condition: restriction on accepted external claims.
Audience: intended recipient of an identity token.
lesson.safety: Use fictional claims only. Never create, download, or paste service-account keys. Authorized resource calls and logging can cost money; test trust boundaries only in approved isolated environments.
cleanup: Retain the fictional trust table.
No keys, tokens, bindings, or identity pools were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a federation provider trusts a shared CI issuer but any repository can deploy. What boundary is missing?
interview_points: Restrict mapped workload attributes and audience.
Scope impersonation separately from resource roles.
Test unauthorized repository and environment claims.
Avoid replacing static keys with equally broad short-lived authority.

gcp/google-cloud-iam-service-accounts-an.core: Federation replaces stored keys with trusted external identity, not automatic resource permission. Restrict issuer and workload claims, distinguish impersonation from target access, and use narrow roles.

storyboard.title: Federation rejects an unapproved repository
storyboard.objective: Show why a trusted issuer alone is insufficient.

scenes.title: Approved workload exchanges identity
scenes.caption: Issuer and workload attributes match the trust design.
scenes.narration: An approved release job presents the expected audience and repository claims before requesting narrowly scoped artifact access.

scenes.title: Different repository attempts access
scenes.caption: A shared issuer does not establish workload approval.
scenes.narration: A token from another repository uses the same issuer but fails the configured workload attribute condition.

scenes.title: Preserve the boundary
scenes.caption: Negative cases remain denied after legitimate access works.
scenes.narration: The trust review verifies approved release claims while retaining explicit rejection of unrelated repositories and environments without issuing static keys.

lesson.title: Google Cloud Storage lifecycle and access
lesson.why: Bucket access, object retention, storage class, and deletion recovery are independent choices. A lifecycle rule that saves apparent capacity can violate retention or increase retrieval charges.
lesson.what: Design an object archive using Cloud Storage IAM, uniform bucket-level access, lifecycle rules, versions, and recovery controls on fictional data.

concepts.name: Access methods need deliberate scope
concepts.body: Uniform bucket-level access uses IAM rather than object ACLs for supported bucket access control. Public access prevention addresses public sharing separately. Signed URLs grant time-limited access to whoever holds them, so treat them as sensitive bearer capabilities rather than ordinary public documentation links.

concepts.name: Objects have generations
concepts.body: An object generation identifies a particular content version. Generation preconditions can prevent overwriting a value that changed since it was read. Object Versioning and soft-delete behavior influence retained data and recovery; deleting the live object may not immediately remove all stored historical bytes.

concepts.name: Lifecycle rules match conditions
concepts.body: Object Lifecycle Management evaluates rules with actions and conditions; all conditions within a rule must match. Changes are asynchronous, not an exact deletion timer. Retention policies and holds can constrain deletion, so eligibility does not automatically mean an object can be removed immediately.

concepts.name: Storage class affects total cost
concepts.body: Classes differ in storage price, retrieval charges, and minimum duration assumptions while retaining online access semantics. Unlike some archive services, Cloud Storage Archive data is available online without a rehydration job. Evaluate requests, retrieval, early deletion, and location-related transfer rather than only stored gigabytes.

e2e: Classify object access, confidentiality, retention, and retrieval frequency.
Choose location, IAM scope, and public-sharing controls independently.
Design generation-aware writes and historical recovery features where needed.
Evaluate lifecycle conditions against synthetic object ages and holds.
Calculate complete retention and retrieval cost components, then plan an isolated restore verification.

tasks.name: Separate access controls
tasks.goal: Avoid an ACL and exposure misconception.
steps: List uniform bucket-level access, IAM, public access prevention, and signed URLs.
Explain that disabling ACL-based access does not itself define the correct IAM policy, and a signed URL must not be casually shared.

tasks.name: Evaluate a lifecycle rule
steps: Assume a rule requires age at least 30 days and prefix logs/. Test logs/a at 45 days, logs/b at 12, and reports/c at 50.
Expected eligibility is only logs/a. A retention hold could still block deletion, and actual lifecycle execution is asynchronous.

tasks.name: Prevent a lost update
steps: Two writers both read generation 7. Require each replacement to match generation 7.
After one succeeds, the other should receive a precondition failure rather than silently overwrite the new generation. This mock does not validate real API behavior.

tasks.name: Review archive economics
steps: Compare rarely read legal records with daily scanned reports. List retrieval and minimum-duration costs that could make the same storage class inappropriate for both.
Do not invent vendor prices; use current published rates only in a later estimate.

key_terms: Generation: identity of an object content version.
Precondition: required state before a mutation.
Uniform bucket-level access: IAM-focused access without object ACLs.
Lifecycle rule: conditional storage transition or deletion action.
Retention hold: restriction preventing eligible data deletion.
lesson.safety: No buckets or signed URLs are created. Storage, operations, retrieval, retained versions, and early deletion may be billable; never test sharing using private documents.
cleanup: Discard synthetic object lists.
Future cleanup must inspect versions, soft-deleted objects, and retention restrictions before claiming a bucket is empty.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a lifecycle rule matches an old object but it remains stored. What would you inspect?
interview_points: Check every rule condition and asynchronous execution.
Inspect holds and retention policies.
Distinguish live, noncurrent, and soft-deleted data.
Review cost without assuming immediate physical deletion.

gcp/google-cloud-storage-lifecycle-and-a.core: Cloud Storage access, generation preconditions, retention, and lifecycle are separate controls. Lifecycle is asynchronous and respects holds. Archive remains online, but retrieval and minimum-duration costs still matter.

storyboard.title: A retention hold prevents lifecycle deletion
storyboard.objective: Connect rule eligibility to independent retention controls.

scenes.title: Object becomes eligible
scenes.caption: Age and prefix conditions both match.
scenes.narration: The retained log generation satisfies the lifecycle rule's age and naming conditions, making it a deletion candidate.

scenes.title: Hold blocks removal
scenes.caption: Lifecycle eligibility does not override retention.
scenes.narration: A separate retention hold prevents deletion, so the object remains stored and can continue contributing to storage usage.

scenes.title: Review authorized retention change
scenes.caption: Removal follows policy, not a forced cleanup shortcut.
scenes.narration: Owners verify legal obligations and authorized hold management before allowing lifecycle processing to remove eligible data asynchronously.

lesson.title: Google Cloud SQL Spanner and Firestore
lesson.why: Relational compatibility, distributed transactions, and document access lead to different database choices. A managed service still requires deliberate schema, consistency, retry, and recovery design.
lesson.what: Compare Cloud SQL, Spanner, and Firestore using a fictional booking application. Focus on transaction boundaries and access patterns rather than claiming one database fits every scale.

concepts.name: Cloud SQL manages familiar engines
concepts.body: Cloud SQL hosts supported relational engines with managed operational features. High-availability configurations and read replicas solve different needs. A regional HA standby supports failover rather than ordinary read scaling; backups remain necessary for logical mistakes that replicate.

concepts.name: Spanner distributes relational work
concepts.body: Spanner combines relational operations with distributed storage and transactions. Its documented serializable transaction mode provides external consistency using TrueTime and coordination. Schema keys, locality, and transaction scope still affect hotspots and latency; distributed SQL does not eliminate physical communication costs.

concepts.name: Firestore models documents
concepts.body: Firestore stores documents in collections and supports indexed queries and atomic transactions. Transaction callbacks can rerun when concurrent changes require retries. Do not perform irreversible external side effects inside a callback as though it executes only once; index and query design also affect cost.

concepts.name: Recovery is service-specific
concepts.body: Availability topology, backup retention, point-in-time recovery, and restore workflows vary by service and configuration. Choose from business RPO and RTO, not a generic managed label. Access controls for server clients and end-user SDKs can differ, so authentication alone is not a complete authorization review.

e2e: List relational constraints, document queries, transaction scope, and regional requirements.
Choose a database family whose supported semantics match those requirements.
Design keys and indexes while anticipating concentrated traffic and query costs.
Implement transaction retry and external-side-effect handling safely.
Plan and later test service-specific backup restoration and client reconnection with synthetic data.

tasks.name: Choose by constraints
steps: Match an existing PostgreSQL application, a distributed relational booking ledger, and a document-centric mobile catalog to candidate services.
Consider Cloud SQL, Spanner, and Firestore respectively, then record compatibility and transaction assumptions instead of declaring automatic winners.

tasks.name: Calculate operation volume
steps: Assume 20,000 sessions/day, each reading eight documents and writing two. Expected daily counts are 160,000 reads and 40,000 writes before retries and index-related costs.
This is a workload calculation, not a Firestore billing quote or a complete invoice model.

tasks.name: Trace a transaction retry
steps: A Firestore transaction callback reads a seat document, sends an email, then conflicts and reruns.
Move email emission outside the retryable callback using a durable outbox or equivalent coordination; the callback must not assume exactly one invocation.

tasks.name: Separate HA and undelete
steps: An accidental booking deletion reaches a replicated database. Explain why failing over to a current copy does not reconstruct deleted history.
Draft an isolated restore and booking-invariant check. Offline reasoning does not prove live consistency, recovery timing, or permissions.

key_terms: External consistency: transaction ordering compatible with real-time ordering under the documented mode.
Document: structured record in Firestore.
Transaction callback: retryable application function computing an atomic update.
HA standby: failover capacity, not necessarily a read endpoint.
Outbox: durable intent record coordinating external effects.
lesson.safety: Do not create databases or send emails. Compute, operations, indexes, replicas, backups, and transfer may cost money; use only invented booking records.
cleanup: Retain the database decision matrix.
No databases or credentials were created; discard synthetic customer identifiers.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a transaction is atomic but an email is sent twice during contention. How can both statements be true?
interview_points: The transaction callback may rerun.
External email is outside database atomicity.
Use durable outbox/idempotency coordination.
Inspect transaction semantics for the chosen service rather than generalizing.

gcp/google-cloud-sql-spanner-and-firesto.core: Cloud SQL emphasizes managed relational engines, Spanner distributed relational transactions, and Firestore document access. Match transaction and query requirements. Retryable callbacks must not perform unguarded external side effects.

storyboard.title: A Firestore transaction callback runs again
storyboard.objective: Separate atomic database writes from external effects.

scenes.title: Read the seat
scenes.caption: The callback computes an update from current data.
scenes.narration: A booking transaction reads the seat document and prepares its write while another client may modify the same data.

scenes.title: Contention causes retry
scenes.caption: The callback cannot assume one invocation.
scenes.narration: A concurrent edit invalidates the initial attempt, so the transaction function reruns; an external email sent inside it could be duplicated.

scenes.title: Coordinate external work durably
scenes.caption: Notification follows a committed intent and deduplication.
scenes.narration: The transaction records a durable notification intent with the booking, and a separate worker sends it using duplicate protection.

lesson.title: Google Kubernetes Engine operations
lesson.why: Automatic cluster management reduces some maintenance work but cannot guarantee an application's disruption tolerance. Workload placement, release channels, identity, and capacity still require explicit decisions.
lesson.what: Compare GKE Standard and Autopilot operations, then plan a node upgrade using a synthetic workload and an offline disruption budget.

concepts.name: Operating modes expose different controls
concepts.body: GKE Standard provides direct control over node pools and many infrastructure choices. Autopilot manages more node and workload infrastructure while enforcing supported constraints. Neither mode removes responsibility for application correctness, resource requests, data retention, and access design.

concepts.name: Regional control planes are not workload replicas
concepts.body: A regional cluster improves control-plane resilience and can distribute node capacity, but a one-replica application remains vulnerable. Topology spread, storage placement, and sufficient ready replicas determine workload survival. Control-plane availability and user-request availability are different metrics.

concepts.name: Release channels organize version movement
concepts.body: Release channels and maintenance settings shape automatic upgrades within supported policies. Control plane, node pools, and add-ons must remain compatible. Maintenance exclusions have scope and limits; they should not be described as permission to keep unsupported versions indefinitely.

concepts.name: Disruption and identity cross layers
concepts.body: Pod disruption budgets constrain voluntary eviction, while surge or blue-green strategies consume replacement capacity. Workload Identity Federation for GKE connects supported Kubernetes identities to Google Cloud authorization, distinct from Kubernetes RBAC. Upgrade tests must include image pulls, identity, networking, and application readiness.

e2e: Inventory cluster mode, location, release channel, versions, and workload owners.
Review deprecated APIs, compatible add-ons, and documented upgrade behavior.
Calculate replica, disruption, and replacement-capacity headroom including storage topology.
Validate a representative canary before broad node replacement.
Observe application errors and scheduling failures, then follow supported recovery procedures if gates fail.

tasks.name: Separate availability layers
steps: Draw a regional control plane with one application replica backed by a zonal volume.
Identify both application replica count and storage topology as remaining risks despite redundant control-plane operation.

tasks.name: Calculate disruption allowance
tasks.goal: Work a bounded offline PDB example.
steps: Assume four healthy replicas and minAvailable three. The modeled voluntary disruption allowance is one.
If one replica becomes unready, allowance becomes zero. Unexpected node failure can still violate availability; the PDB does not prevent it.

tasks.name: Review maintenance assumptions
steps: A team proposes excluding all upgrades forever. Reject the unsupported assumption and require review of release-channel and exclusion limits.
Record application compatibility tests and an owner for upcoming API removals.

tasks.name: Plan a canary upgrade
steps: Require synthetic application requests, image access, workload identity, volume attachment, and network checks before expanding.
Document recovery from a failed gate. Offline manifests and arithmetic do not prove GKE scheduling, federation, or actual upgrade behavior.

key_terms: Autopilot: GKE mode managing more infrastructure automatically.
Standard: GKE mode exposing node-pool management controls.
Release channel: policy grouping for version availability and upgrades.
Topology spread: placement constraint distributing replicas.
PDB: bound on voluntary application disruption.
lesson.safety: Do not create or upgrade clusters. Compute, workload resources, storage, networking, and logs can cost money; never drain shared workloads or alter production maintenance settings.
cleanup: Retain the synthetic upgrade gates.
Future cluster cleanup must inspect persistent disks, load balancers, and retained snapshots independently.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a regional GKE cluster stays reachable while its application is unavailable during maintenance. Why is that possible?
interview_points: Control-plane resilience is separate from workload replicas.
Inspect PDBs, topology, readiness, and zonal storage.
Check surge capacity and version compatibility.
Measure user requests rather than cluster API uptime alone.

gcp/google-kubernetes-engine-operations.core: GKE operating mode and release channel shape infrastructure management, not application correctness. Regional control planes need resilient workloads beneath them. Budget disruption and replacement capacity, then validate identity, storage, networking, and service behavior.

storyboard.title: GKE maintenance exposes a single application replica
storyboard.objective: Separate managed control-plane health from user availability.

scenes.title: Healthy cluster and application
scenes.caption: One running replica masks a placement weakness.
scenes.narration: The regional control plane is available and the application serves traffic, but only one pod supplies its user-facing capacity.

scenes.title: Node maintenance interrupts service
scenes.caption: Control-plane health cannot replace missing ready replicas.
scenes.narration: The node update displaces the lone pod, creating application downtime even while Kubernetes management requests continue to succeed.

scenes.title: Design workload resilience
scenes.caption: Replicas and topology accompany supported upgrades.
scenes.narration: The team adds justified replica and placement headroom, reviews storage constraints, and verifies readiness during the next controlled maintenance rehearsal.

lesson.title: Google Cloud Run and event-driven functions
lesson.why: Serverless concurrency can improve utilization or overwhelm a non-thread-safe application. Event-driven delivery also introduces retries, so compute simplicity must not hide correctness and dependency limits.
lesson.what: Model a Cloud Run service and event-driven function using explicit concurrency, request duration, revision, identity, and retry assumptions without deploying containers.

concepts.name: Services and jobs have different lifecycles
concepts.body: Cloud Run services handle requests using container instances and revisions. Jobs run bounded tasks to completion rather than serving an HTTP endpoint. Cloud Run functions provides a function-oriented experience with supported triggers; generation and trigger choices affect capabilities and delivery behavior.

concepts.name: Concurrency changes per-instance demand
concepts.body: Maximum concurrency bounds simultaneous requests per instance but is not a throughput guarantee. CPU, memory, blocking I/O, and application thread safety determine usable concurrency. Defaults can vary by deployment method and configuration, so set and document requirements instead of relying on a memorized constant.

concepts.name: Autoscaling has dependency consequences
concepts.body: New instances take time to initialize. Minimum instances can reduce startup exposure while adding cost; maximum-instance settings help bound resources but do not create perfect global downstream admission control. Request duration and retry traffic affect required capacity and database connection pressure.

concepts.name: Events require duplicate-safe work
concepts.body: Event-driven handlers should use stable event or business identifiers and durable completion state. An instance can fail after committing an external effect but before acknowledgement. Revision rollout and retry policies must preserve compatible event schemas and avoid repeating irreversible actions.

e2e: Choose request-serving, job, or function execution from the workload lifecycle.
Make startup deterministic and use supported runtime identity for dependencies.
Select concurrency and scaling bounds from application behavior and downstream budgets.
Deploy a hypothetical immutable revision and verify synthetic requests or events.
Use bounded retries, idempotency, and observed latency to guide rollout and recovery.

tasks.name: Choose an execution shape
steps: Compare an HTTP API, a nightly finite export, and a storage-event handler.
Consider a Cloud Run service, job, and supported event-driven function respectively; document runtime and trigger requirements before selecting.

tasks.name: Calculate active requests
steps: Assume 240 requests/second and 0.5-second mean duration. Average active requests are 120.
At a hypothetical usable concurrency of 20 per instance, the arithmetic floor is six instances before headroom and scaling behavior. This is not a guaranteed autoscaler outcome.

tasks.name: Test thread-safety assumptions
steps: A container stores the current user's ID in a process-global variable. Explain how two concurrent requests can overwrite each other's context.
Use request-scoped state; setting concurrency one can reduce this specific overlap but is not a complete security design.

tasks.name: Handle a retried event
steps: A handler writes a completion record and crashes before returning. On retry, check the stable export ID and durable result.
This mock does not prove actual event delivery, IAM authorization, or Cloud Run scaling.

key_terms: Revision: immutable service configuration and image version.
Concurrency: requests active on one instance.
Job: finite task execution rather than request serving.
Cold start: initialization before useful processing.
Idempotency: preserving one intended effect across repeats.
lesson.safety: Do not deploy or invoke services. CPU, memory, requests, minimum instances, builds, logs, and downstream operations can incur costs; never embed credentials in container images.
cleanup: Retain concurrency and dependency assumptions.
No revisions, jobs, functions, or artifacts were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, increasing Cloud Run concurrency lowers instance count but causes incorrect user responses. What would you inspect?
interview_points: Check thread safety and request-scoped state.
Measure memory, CPU, and dependency saturation.
Treat concurrency as a bound, not guaranteed throughput.
Keep event retries and business idempotency separate.

gcp/google-cloud-run-and-event-driven-fu.core: Cloud Run concurrency controls simultaneous work per instance, not guaranteed throughput. Choose services, jobs, or functions by lifecycle; protect request state, downstream capacity, and repeated event effects.

storyboard.title: Cloud Run concurrency reveals shared-state bugs
storyboard.objective: Connect request overlap to application isolation.

scenes.title: Single-request assumption
scenes.caption: A global variable appears harmless at low overlap.
scenes.narration: The application serves a quiet request stream, concealing its incorrect use of process-global state for the current user.

scenes.title: Requests overlap
scenes.caption: One request can overwrite another's context.
scenes.narration: Higher concurrency sends multiple requests to the same instance, exposing shared-state corruption even though the platform remains healthy.

scenes.title: Isolate and measure
scenes.caption: Correct request state precedes concurrency tuning.
scenes.narration: The application adopts request-scoped context and tests representative overlap before choosing a concurrency setting that meets latency and resource budgets.

lesson.title: Google Pub Sub delivery ordering and retries
lesson.why: Messaging guarantees have specific scopes. An acknowledged message, a successfully committed business update, and a publisher's unique logical event are not automatically the same thing.
lesson.what: Design Pub/Sub subscribers with acknowledgement deadlines, ordering keys, retry handling, and deliberate use of exactly-once delivery where supported.

concepts.name: Subscriptions own delivery progress
concepts.body: A topic receives published messages and subscriptions maintain independent delivery state. A subscriber acknowledges after processing, while acknowledgement deadlines and extensions affect redelivery. Multiple subscriptions each receive their own copy of the stream; more consumers on one subscription share its work.

concepts.name: Ordering is scoped
concepts.body: Ordering keys can preserve order for messages sharing a key under documented publishing and subscription requirements. They do not impose global ordering across unrelated keys. One slow ordered key can constrain its progress, so choose a business scope that does not unnecessarily serialize all traffic.

concepts.name: Exactly-once has boundaries
concepts.body: Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery applies to supported pull subscriptions within a cloud region and uses Pub/Sub message IDs. Push and export subscriptions do not support that feature. It provides acknowledgement-related guarantees, not automatic deduplication of a publisher sending the same logical event twice as separate messages.

concepts.name: External effects still need coordination
concepts.body: A consumer may commit a database update before its acknowledgement succeeds. Track processing progress until successful acknowledgement and use durable business idempotency. Dead-letter forwarding and retry policies aid recovery but do not repair malformed messages or guarantee every replay is harmless.

e2e: Define stable business event identity and the required ordering scope.
Choose subscription type and documented delivery features that fit the consumers.
Set processing deadlines, flow control, and acknowledgement-extension behavior.
Persist effects and progress safely before acknowledging successful work.
Monitor backlog age, expired deadlines, and failures, then replay under bounded duplicate protection.

tasks.name: Separate subscriber groups
steps: An audit pipeline and an email pipeline each need every event. Give them separate subscriptions.
Workers within the email pipeline can share its subscription; explain why adding a worker is not the same as adding another independent subscriber group.

tasks.name: Calculate lease risk
steps: Assume a ten-second acknowledgement deadline and a handler that takes 18 seconds, with no extension.
The handler exceeds the deadline by eight seconds, so redelivery is possible. Add supported lease extension or redesign processing; this arithmetic is not a live delivery test.

tasks.name: Challenge exactly-once claims
tasks.goal: Distinguish message IDs and business IDs.
steps: A publisher sends order O twice as two messages with different Pub/Sub message IDs.
Even supported exactly-once delivery does not merge those logical duplicates automatically. Require order-level idempotency.

tasks.name: Rehearse a failed acknowledgement
steps: A consumer commits O but acknowledgement fails. Preserve completion state and use the latest valid acknowledgement information on subsequent delivery.
These mocks do not prove actual ordering, regional guarantees, retries, or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Subscription: independent message delivery state.
Acknowledgement deadline: lease interval before possible redelivery.
Ordering key: scope for ordered message processing.
Message ID: Pub/Sub-assigned identity of a published message.
Business idempotency key: identity of the logical operation.
lesson.safety: Do not publish messages. Throughput, retention, replay, and downstream work can incur costs; never test with actual payment or notification events.
cleanup: Discard synthetic order and message IDs.
No subscriptions, topics, or dead-letter destinations were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an order is processed twice despite exactly-once delivery being enabled. What questions clarify the guarantee?
interview_points: Verify supported pull subscription and regional scope.
Compare Pub/Sub message IDs with business order IDs.
Inspect acknowledgement success and durable progress.
Coordinate external effects rather than assuming a cross-system transaction.

gcp/google-pub-sub-delivery-ordering-and.core: Pub/Sub ordering and exactly-once delivery have documented scopes. Supported regional pull delivery does not deduplicate separately published business events or atomically include a database. Preserve durable progress and business idempotency.

storyboard.title: Two Pub/Sub messages represent one business order
storyboard.objective: Separate broker message identity from logical operation identity.

scenes.title: First logical order
scenes.caption: A broker message carries a stable order identifier.
scenes.narration: The publisher emits an order event, and the subscriber processes it while retaining the business identifier separately from the message ID.

scenes.title: Publisher repeats the order
scenes.caption: A new message ID can carry the same business event.
scenes.narration: A publish retry creates another message for the same order, outside the meaning of deduplicating one message's successful delivery.

scenes.title: Deduplicate the business effect
scenes.caption: Consumer correctness uses the order identifier.
scenes.narration: The consumer recognizes the prior order completion, acknowledges the new delivery, and avoids creating a second business transaction.

lesson.title: Google Cloud Logging Monitoring and Trace
lesson.why: A graph, a log entry, and a trace answer different operational questions. Collection gaps and aggregation choices can make a seemingly healthy dashboard misleading.
lesson.what: Connect Cloud Logging routing, Cloud Monitoring time series, and Cloud Trace request context using fabricated observations rather than querying live telemetry.

concepts.name: Logging routes structured evidence
concepts.body: Cloud Logging receives entries with resource and severity metadata. Log sinks route matching entries to configured destinations; exclusions and retention shape what remains queryable. A sink is not automatically a retroactive export of every historical entry, and destinations require appropriate writer permissions.

concepts.name: Monitoring summarizes time series
concepts.body: Metrics describe numerical behavior over time with labels and monitored-resource context. Alignment periods and cross-series reducers change the meaning of charts. Averaging instance percentages can misrepresent service-wide error ratios when instances serve different traffic volumes.

concepts.name: Trace links request work
concepts.body: Distributed traces connect spans using propagated context so latency can be attributed across services. Sampling reduces collection volume but limits visibility into individual requests. A missing span can indicate missing propagation or instrumentation rather than proof that a dependency was never called.

concepts.name: Operations need bounded evidence
concepts.body: Alert policies require thresholds, evaluation duration, notification ownership, and missing-data treatment. High-cardinality labels and verbose logs increase cost. Protect user identifiers and tokens, and correlate observations before claiming causality; temporal proximity alone is not an experiment.

e2e: Define customer-facing success and latency signals before choosing dashboard widgets.
Instrument structured logs and trace context without sensitive payloads.
Configure sink filters, destination permissions, metric labels, and retention.
Investigate a bounded incident window by joining resource and trace identifiers.
Verify mitigation through service-level outcomes and record unresolved collection gaps.

tasks.name: Choose the signal
steps: Use metrics for aggregate failure rate, logs for structured error details, and traces for time spent in dependencies.
Document what data is actually collected rather than assuming every product automatically observes every application path.

tasks.name: Calculate the weighted error ratio
steps: Instance A serves 900 requests with nine errors; B serves 100 with ten errors.
Correct service error ratio is (9 + 10) / (900 + 100) = 1.9%, not the unweighted average of 1% and 10%, which is 5.5%.

tasks.name: Review a sink failure
steps: Logs appear in the source context but not the intended destination. Inspect sink filter, creation timing, destination support, and writer permissions.
Do not infer the application stopped logging simply from one empty destination.

tasks.name: Trace missing context
steps: An API span has no downstream child span despite a logged external request. Investigate propagation, instrumentation, sampling, and clock context.
These fabricated records do not prove a real incident, delivery guarantee, or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Log sink: filter and destination rule for log routing.
Time series: metric values with consistent label identity.
Reducer: aggregation across multiple series.
Span: timed operation within a distributed trace.
Trace context: identifiers linking operations across service boundaries.
lesson.safety: Do not query production logs or add sinks. Ingestion, storage, queries, exports, and high-cardinality metrics may incur costs; never route sensitive telemetry to unapproved destinations.
cleanup: Discard fabricated telemetry rows.
Retain the signal definitions; no log-routing or alert configuration changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, two instances show 1% and 10% errors. Why is 5.5% not necessarily the application's error rate?
interview_points: Weight by actual request counts.
Check alignment windows and label scope.
Distinguish missing telemetry from zero errors.
Use traces and logs for diagnosis after measuring impact.

gcp/google-cloud-logging-monitoring-and-.core: Logging routes event evidence, Monitoring aggregates numerical signals, and Trace links request work. Use weighted service ratios, deliberate retention and routing, and explicit sampling assumptions before drawing conclusions.

storyboard.title: A log sink misses its intended destination
storyboard.objective: Separate source collection from routing and access.

scenes.title: Source logs arrive
scenes.caption: Collection succeeds before destination routing.
scenes.narration: The application emits structured records that enter Cloud Logging with resource labels and a correlation identifier.

scenes.title: Destination stays empty
scenes.caption: Filters or writer permissions can block the next step.
scenes.narration: The sink cannot route matching records as intended, so an empty destination does not prove the application emitted nothing.

scenes.title: Repair the routing contract
scenes.caption: Confirm approved scope and permissions without broad export.
scenes.narration: Operators review the filter and destination writer identity, then verify newly routed synthetic entries while preserving privacy and retention policy.

lesson.title: Google Cloud KMS Secret Manager and organization policy
lesson.why: Rotating a key version, publishing a secret version, and enforcing resource constraints are different operations. None automatically repairs every dependent application's credentials or access policy.
lesson.what: Map Cloud KMS, Secret Manager, and Organization Policy responsibilities for a fictional database application, including recovery dependencies and least-privilege administration.

concepts.name: KMS keys contain versions
concepts.body: Cloud KMS manages cryptographic keys and versions. Symmetric rotation can create a new primary version for future encryption, but existing ciphertext is not automatically reencrypted. Asymmetric rotation has different support and requires deliberate handling; verify algorithm and key-purpose requirements.

concepts.name: Secret versions store values
concepts.body: Secret Manager separates secret metadata from versioned secret payloads. Adding a version does not by itself change a database password or refresh every application's cache. A safe rotation workflow coordinates the target credential, version selection, client refresh, validation, and any permitted rollback.

concepts.name: Organization Policy constrains configuration
concepts.body: Organization Policy applies supported constraints across the resource hierarchy, limiting how resources may be configured. IAM separately governs who can perform operations. Constraint inheritance, enforcement scope, exceptions, and service support matter; a project owner cannot assume local IAM grants bypass all organization restrictions.

concepts.name: Recovery requires old dependencies
concepts.body: Retained backups may depend on older KMS versions. Disabling or destroying required material can make recovery impossible despite intact backup bytes. Review access, audit records, key state, retention obligations, and application behavior before retiring versions or changing secret access.

e2e: Inventory encrypted data, key versions, secret consumers, and configuration constraints.
Separate cryptographic use, secret access, and administrative permissions.
Design coordinated secret rotation and version-aware key lifecycle controls.
Test policy changes in a limited scope with documented expected denials.
Verify application and backup recovery before retiring old versions or widening enforcement.

tasks.name: Map control responsibilities
tasks.goal: Avoid substituting one control for another.
steps: Assign encrypting a data key to KMS, retrieving a database password to Secret Manager, and restricting resource configuration to Organization Policy.
State the separate IAM authorization needed for each action.

tasks.name: Work a key-dependency decision
steps: Assume backup B was encrypted with key version 3, while version 4 is now primary. The proposed cleanup destroys version 3.
Expected decision: block destruction until B's retention and recoverability are resolved. Making version 4 primary does not automatically reencrypt B.

tasks.name: Trace secret-cache mismatch
steps: A new secret version exists but the database still accepts only the old password. Explain why publishing metadata is not completed credential rotation.
Draft target update, client refresh, authentication validation, and failure recovery steps without actual secret values.

tasks.name: Review a policy rollout
steps: A constraint is proposed at organization scope. First document supported resource effects, inherited behavior, exceptions, and a canary project.
These mock reviews do not prove live KMS, Secret Manager, IAM, or policy behavior.

key_terms: Key version: particular cryptographic material within a key.
Primary version: symmetric key version selected for new encryption.
Secret version: stored revision of a sensitive value.
Constraint: Organization Policy rule governing supported configuration.
Cryptographic destruction: removal of material needed for decryption or signing.
lesson.safety: Do not retrieve secrets or modify key states. Cryptographic requests, versions, secrets, and telemetry may be billable; destroying required key material can permanently prevent recovery.
cleanup: Keep only fictional dependency identifiers.
No secret material or credentials were accessed, and no policies were applied.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a team rotates its primary KMS version and wants to destroy all older versions. What is the recovery risk?
interview_points: Existing ciphertext can still depend on old versions.
Inventory backups and retained objects before destruction.
Distinguish rotation from reencryption and secret replacement.
Review IAM and organization constraints separately.

gcp/google-cloud-kms-secret-manager-and-.core: KMS versions protect cryptographic material; Secret Manager versions hold credential values; Organization Policy constrains configuration. Rotation does not automatically reencrypt history or update target passwords. Preserve recovery dependencies.

storyboard.title: An old KMS version remains necessary for backups
storyboard.objective: Connect rotation to retained ciphertext dependencies.

scenes.title: New encryption uses new primary
scenes.caption: Rotation changes future encryption selection.
scenes.narration: The key's primary version changes while retained backup ciphertext continues referencing the material used when it was encrypted.

scenes.title: Old version is proposed for destruction
scenes.caption: Intact backup bytes may become unreadable.
scenes.narration: Destroying the required version would break the backup's decryption dependency, so rotation alone is insufficient cleanup evidence.

scenes.title: Retain or migrate deliberately
scenes.caption: Recovery obligations determine version retirement.
scenes.narration: Owners verify retention and restore requirements, preserve necessary key material, and authorize retirement only after dependent data is safely handled.
